introduction: Xenophon, Hiero 9.1–11 and 11.1–15. 307 Greek words in 6 paragraphs.

Based on Hiero 9 and 11. Simonides’ recommendations are adapted into a connected argument. The dialogue does not establish that the historical Hiero implemented them; the final questions are course reflection.

Read once for the argument, then translate paragraph by paragraph. Try each paragraph before opening glosses; finish the final two paragraphs as connected prose. Submit your connected English translation using the reading submission box.

The vocabulary panel separates new required entries from review words. Paragraph glosses supply additional reading support; a gloss alone does not make a word or an advanced construction a production requirement.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Σιμωνίδης τῷ Ἱέρωνι περὶ ἀρχῆς διαλέγεται. ὁ μὲν Ἱέρων τύραννός ἐστιν, ὁ δὲ Σιμωνίδης ποιητής. οὐ μέντοι περὶ ᾠδῆς μόνον λέγουσιν, ἀλλὰ περὶ τοῦ βίου τοῦ ἄρχοντος. ὁ Ἱέρων πολλὰ κτήματα ἔχει, ἀλλὰ φοβεῖται καὶ οὐ πάντας τοὺς πλησίον πιστοὺς νομίζει. τὸ πλείω ἔχειν οὐ πάντως τὸ ἥδιον ζῆν παρέχει.

Ὁ Σιμωνίδης ἄλλην ὁδὸν δείκνυσιν. ὁ ἄρχων μὴ μόνον τὸν ἴδιον οἶκον πλουσιώτερον ποιείτω, ἀλλὰ τὴν πόλιν ἀμείνω. ὅταν οἱ πολῖται καλῶς πράττωσιν, ὁ ἄρχων μείζονα τιμὴν λαμβάνει. τὰ γὰρ κοινὰ ἔργα πλείοσιν ἀνθρώποις ὠφέλιμά ἐστιν ἢ τὰ ἴδια κτήματα. οὐ τὸ μέγιστον ἀργύριον μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ εὔνοια δύναμιν παρέχει.

Ἐπιμελοῦ οὖν ὅπως οἱ πολῖται ἐργάσονται καὶ τὰς τέχνας ἀσκήσουσιν. ἆθλα δίδου τοῖς εὖ ποιοῦσιν, ἵνα καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι πονεῖν ἐθέλωσιν. οἱ μὲν γεωργοὶ τὴν γῆν βελτίω ποιήσουσιν, οἱ δὲ τὰ κοινὰ ἔργα κοσμήσουσιν. τὸ γὰρ ἆθλον πολλάκις μικρότερόν ἐστι τῆς δαπάνης ἣν οἱ ἀγωνιζόμενοι ἑκόντες ποιοῦνται. οὕτως ἡ φιλοτιμία πρὸς τὸ κοινὸν συμφέρον ἄγει.

paragraphs.greek: Σκόπει δὲ ὅπως οἱ φύλακες τοὺς πολίτας φυλάξουσιν, οὐ μόνον σέ. ὁ γὰρ φόβος οὐχ ὁμοῖός ἐστι τῇ φιλίᾳ. ὅταν οἱ ἄνθρωποι τὴν δύναμιν πρὸς αὑτοὺς ὠφέλιμον ὁρῶσιν, ἧττον αὐτὴν φοβοῦνται. ὁ ἄριστος ἄρχων οὐ τῷ ἰδιώτῃ περὶ πλούτου ἀγωνίζεται, ἀλλὰ ταῖς ἄλλαις πόλεσι περὶ τῆς τῶν πολιτῶν εὐδαιμονίας.

Ταῦτα ὁ Σιμωνίδης συμβουλεύει. ὁ δὲ ἀναγνώστης ζητεῖ τίς τῶν προτάσεων ὠφελεῖται. ὁ γεωργὸς λαμβάνει τιμήν, ἡ πόλις πλείονα ἔργα, ὁ δὲ ἄρχων ἀσφαλεστέραν ἀρχήν. ἀλλὰ τίς κρίνει τὸν ἄρχοντα; τίς τῷ ἀδικούμενῳ βοηθεῖ; ταῦτα δεῖ ἐξετάζειν πρὶν τὴν εὐεργεσίαν τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ ταὐτὴν νομίζειν. ἡ γὰρ τῶν κτημάτων αὔξησις οὐ πᾶσαν περὶ τοῦ δικαίου ἐρώτησιν λύει.

Τὸν λόγον οὖν ὡς συμβουλὴν ἀναγινώσκωμεν, οὐχ ὡς μαρτυρίαν ὅτι πάντα οὕτως ἐγένετο. ὁ συγγραφεὺς δύο φωνὰς ἡμῖν παρέχει, ἵνα συγκρίνωμεν τὸ φοβεῖσθαι καὶ τὸ φιλεῖσθαι. ἡ τοῦ ἄρχοντος εὐδαιμονία πρὸς τὴν τῆς πόλεως εὐδαιμονίαν ἀναφέρεται· ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τῆς ἐξουσίας μέτρον ἔτι ζητητέον ἐστίν.

reading.translation:
Simonides discusses rule with Hiero. Hiero is a tyrant, Simonides a poet. Yet they speak not only about song but about the ruler’s life. Hiero has many possessions, but he is afraid and does not consider everyone nearby trustworthy. Having more does not necessarily provide a more pleasant life.

Simonides points out another path. Let the ruler make not only his own household wealthier but the city better. Whenever the citizens prosper, the ruler receives greater honor. For public works benefit more people than private possessions do. Not only the greatest amount of silver but also goodwill provides power.

Take care, then, that the citizens will work and practice their crafts. Give prizes to those doing well, so that others too may be willing to labor. Farmers will improve the land, while others will adorn public works. For the prize is often smaller than the expense that competitors willingly incur. In this way ambition leads toward the common advantage.

See that the guards will protect the citizens, not only you. Fear is not the same as friendship. Whenever people see power as beneficial to themselves, they fear it less. The best ruler does not compete with a private individual in wealth, but with other cities over the well-being of his citizens.

Simonides gives this advice. The reader asks who benefits from the proposals. The farmer receives honor, the city more works, and the ruler a safer rule. But who judges the ruler? Who helps the person wronged? We must examine these questions before treating benefaction as identical with justice. For an increase in possessions does not resolve every question about what is just.

Let us therefore read the argument as advice, not as testimony that everything happened in this way. The author supplies two voices so that we may compare being feared and being loved. The ruler’s well-being is related to the city’s well-being; but the measure of his authority still requires examination.

body: Read these related expressions in the lesson’s argument. κοινός means “common, shared”; ἴδιος means “private, one’s own”; συμφέρον means “advantage”.
Explain which expression fits an action, a person, or an evaluation. A shared root connects meanings but does not make the words interchangeable in a sentence.

sections.title: 1. Regular and irregular comparison
body: Regular comparatives commonly use -τερος and superlatives -τατος: σοφός, σοφώτερος, σοφώτατος. Learn the whole adjective and accent. Some frequent comparisons use other stems: ἀγαθός can give ἀμείνων/ἄριστος or βελτίων/βέλτιστος; μέγας gives μείζων/μέγιστος, and πολύς gives πλείων/πλεῖστος. Their shades of meaning depend on context.

A comparative can compare with an explicit standard, imply “rather/too,” or contrast two alternatives. A superlative can mean the highest in a group or intensively “very.” Thus σοφώτατος need not always assert that someone is the wisest person in the world.

sections.title: 2. Comparatives in -ων and -ον
body: Comparatives such as μείζων have masculine/feminine nominative singular -ων and neuter -ον. The n-stem produces genitive μείζονος, dative μείζονι, and accusative masculine/feminine μείζονα. Neuter nominative and accusative agree: μεῖζον. Learn the accent as part of the form.

Contracted alternatives coexist with n-stem forms: accusative singular μείζω alongside μείζονα, plural masculine/feminine μείζους alongside μείζονες/μείζονας, and neuter plural μείζω alongside μείζονα. A form such as ἀμείνω can therefore be accusative singular masculine/feminine or neuter plural. Agreement and context resolve it.

sections.title: 3. Standards of comparison and adverbs
body: A comparative can take a genitive standard: μείζων τῆς οἰκίας, “larger than the house.” With ἤ, keep the compared items parallel in construction: σοφώτερος ἢ ὁ ἀδελφός. Distinguish the comparative’s standard from a possessive genitive elsewhere in the sentence.

Adverbs commonly use neuter singular comparative and neuter plural superlative: σοφῶς, σοφώτερον, σοφώτατα. Common irregular forms include εὖ, ἄμεινον/βέλτιον, ἄριστα/βέλτιστα, and μάλα, μᾶλλον, μάλιστα. Comparison can express degree of an action as well as a quality of a noun.

sections.title: 4. Care and effort: ὅπως with future indicative
body: Verbs of care and effort can take an object clause with ὅπως and future indicative: ἐπιμελοῦ ὅπως οἱ φύλακες φυλάξουσιν, “Take care that the guards will protect.” The clause states the result one is to see to. A negative object clause uses ὅπως μή. The future is a finite indicative, not a subjunctive merely because ὅπως appears.

Compare a purpose clause: ἆθλα δίδωσιν ἵνα οἱ πολῖται πονῶσιν, “He gives prizes so that the citizens may work.” First identify the governing verb and clause function, then the form. A ruler’s intention, a plan requiring effort, and an achieved result remain three different claims.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Hiero
body: Hiero is a compact dialogue in eleven chapters between Hiero, ruler of Syracuse in Sicily, and the poet Simonides. It begins with an apparently enviable position: a ruler possesses wealth, servants, and power. Simonides asks how that life compares with private life. Hiero’s answers expose the anxieties behind the privilege—distrust, danger, distorted relationships, and uncertainty about whether praise is sincere. The conversation asks what it would take for power to produce happiness rather than fear.

The later chapters change direction. Simonides proposes ways to connect the ruler’s interests with the community’s prosperity: reward useful achievement, promote productive work, and make public success a source of honor. The argument does not simply equate wealth with justice. It invites the reader to test whether a ruler can win willing support by benefiting others and whether such benefits resolve the deeper problem of unaccountable authority. The ruler and the community remain distinct parties whose interests may overlap without becoming identical.

Read the work as a crafted inquiry into tyranny and leadership. The historical Hiero I belongs to fifth-century Syracuse; Xenophon wrote later. The dialogue is not a transcript of a recoverable meeting and does not prove that Hiero adopted Simonides’ program. Begin with the complaints in chapters 1–7, then compare the proposals in chapters 8–11. Ask who speaks at each turn, what assumptions each speaker challenges, and why the work ends with advice rather than a narrative showing the advice put into practice. In this lesson, chapters 9 and 11 supply the selected proposals, while the complete English translation lets you examine the argument that leads to them.

sections.title: A tyrant’s prosperity problem
body: In the Hiero, Simonides redirects attention from the ruler’s private possessions to the community’s prosperity. Prizes, productive work, and public benefit become ways to seek honor. The question is not merely whether a ruler can afford generous gifts, but whether the conditions of rule can produce trust.

A prize can induce people to spend effort far beyond the value of the reward. That insight makes the proposals practical, but also invites scrutiny. Who chooses the winning activity? Who can compete? Who provides labor while someone else receives honor? The dialogue’s advice leaves room for these questions.

sections.title: Syracuse and the literary setting
body: Hiero I ruled Syracuse in the fifth century BCE. Xenophon’s dialogue was written later and uses a conversation with Simonides to explore tyranny. It is not a record proving that the ruler implemented a public program. Keep the historical setting separate from the dialogue’s imagined argumentative occasion.

“Tyrant” in Greek political vocabulary identifies a kind of sole rule; the ethical evaluation still requires attention to the actual argument. The work examines fear and dependence even while proposing reform. Benefaction can improve a community without answering every question about accountability.

sections.title: Allocate a civic budget
body: Imagine a small fund that can support agriculture, a festival, or a public amenity. Allocate it and name the beneficiaries, the workers, and the people excluded from the decision. This is a classroom simulation, not a reconstruction of Syracusan accounts. Compare your allocation with Simonides’ priorities.

Translate the comparative claims and the ὅπως clauses, then give a continuous version of the last two paragraphs. Explain the difference between “take care that they will...” and “do this so that they may...”. End with one question that a satisfied beneficiary might still ask a powerful ruler.

questions.prompt: Why can a prize be economically effective?
questions.answer: It may encourage effort beyond its own cost.
